summary: A free coding font's site built as a single-screen, keyboard-driven terminal-like app: ten numbered sections, all set small in the font on flat grey, driven by arrows, number keys and letter shortcuts. It teaches its Smart Kerning idea, tests the reader with a character-guessing game, and builds a personalised font in the browser. Only section 01 was captured as an image; sections 02–10 come from dom.html.

instances.look: A flat mid-grey screen with black 12–24px mono text, a row of numbered section tabs on top and a legend of keycaps along the bottom. No images, no display sizes: it resembles a terminal or an old manual
instances.feel: A tool for programmers, not a page about one
instances.ux: No scrolling: ↑↓←→ move focus between controls, 1 2 3… jump to sections, WASD scrolls inside a section, + − zoom, ENTER/ESC edit text, R reset, B L I weight and italic, M light/dark, C high contrast, H hides keys. All state restyles the whole site live. Mobile shows a warning to use desktop for all features
instances.learn: Make navigation part of the pitch: a site driven like an editor proves to programmers that the designer thinks like them, and global shortcuts turn every paragraph into a specimen

reconstruction.layout: Fixed 1440×900 app; tab strip at top from x≈28, 10 labels ~90px apart with the active one in a darker chip; one visible section at a time in the left two-thirds (#main_scale scales for zoom); keyboard legend pinned to the bottom 55px
reconstruction.typography: All Commit Mono: title and tagline 24px Regular; body 12px Regular, leading ~1.3; legend 10–12px; keycaps are outlined boxes ~14px
reconstruction.behaviour: Global keydown handler; tabs are radio inputs (nav_form, .nav_section_input) so Tab order and arrow focus work natively; showing a section adds .visible; a #click_focus overlay asks for a click when the window loses focus; #change_setting briefly confirms each setting change; #block_tab_start and #block_tab_end trap focus; 'loading' text at t≈0.3s while the font loads
reconstruction.content: 'Use keyboard to control website', tips such as 'Tip: Press I to switch between italic and regular' seeded in each section
reconstruction.html: #app_root > #click_focus, #change_setting, #page_animation, #loading, #content_root > header > nav > form#nav_form + #keyboard_section; #main_scale > section#section_1…10; .key[data-key-code] for pressed-state feedback; forms use data-forform and onchange=updateX(event,this)

instances.ux: The first thing taught is the shortcuts; there is no buy or download button
instances.learn: For a font selling neutrality, an anti-hero fits: replace the display moment with operating instructions

reconstruction.behaviour: Next section button moves focus and section
reconstruction.content: 'Commit Mono is an anonymous and neutral coding font focused on creating a better reading experience.'

instances.look: Section 02 'Concept', HTML only: 'The most effective font is the one you don't notice.' with a four-part list of what the font refuses to do
instances.ux: Text with a tip: press I for italic
instances.learn: State the design by negation: listing what the font refuses to do is a stronger brief than listing its features

reconstruction.layout: Same left column as section 01, heading then a short paragraph, ~500px wide
reconstruction.typography: Heading 24px Commit Mono Regular; body 12px; tip line at the end
reconstruction.content: 'No super high x-height, no geometric construction, no eye-catching design and no confusing ligatures. Designed to be neutral and anonymous, Commit Mono is quietly useful.'

instances.look: Section 02, HTML only: the 96 printable ASCII characters in a real table whose rows and columns are headed by binary (000–111, 0000–1111), each cell a radio input, captioned 'Commit Mono: ASCII character table'
instances.ux: Arrow keys or clicks move a selection through the cells (updateTable); what it updates beyond the selection is not visible in the archive
instances.learn: Lay out the character set by binary code, not alphabetically: the table's headers speak the audience's language

reconstruction.content: ASCII 0x20–0x7F, plus prose: 'Since most code is written using ASCII characters, these characters are the backbone of every coding font.'
reconstruction.html: form#table_form > table > tr > th (binary labels), td > input[type=radio] + label

instances.look: Section 03 'Familiar', HTML only: a timeline of five years (1896, 1956, 2013, 2017, 2023) with an SVG letter sample for each, and a note on what was taken from each model

instances.learn: Give each ancestor a verdict and a borrowed trait ('Clear, simple and monospaced, but too quirky'): the lineage becomes an argument for the new font

reconstruction.layout: Row of 5 radio-backed year stops, an SVG sample per year, and one text area beneath

reconstruction.content: 'Franklin Gothic, 1896. Tried-and-true, but overly traditional for code. Inspiration was taken from most of the letter constructions, such as g.'
reconstruction.assets: 5 SVG specimens traced from the reference fonts

instances.look: Section 04 'Intelligent', HTML only: 'Commit Mono: Normal programming typeface' set twice, with four radios (Smart kerning OFF/ON, How it works OFF/ON). The 'How it works' view zooms into the letters m o i and shows the o slid 44 units
instances.ux: Keyboard or click toggles the sample between plain and kerned; a second pair shows the mechanism on three letters
instances.learn: Two toggles for one feature: first show the effect, then the mechanism on the smallest example possible

reconstruction.layout: Radio row, then a sample line, then an explanation swapped per state; 'm o i' shown large with the letter boxes
reconstruction.typography: Sample ~24–32px Commit Mono with ss05 on or off; explanation 12px
reconstruction.behaviour: form#intelligent_form onchange=updateIntelligent; select_state = before, after, original, …; the switch is the font's ss05 smart-kerning feature
reconstruction.content: 'Smart kerning works by looking at single letter between two other letters. If the other letters are in different width classes, the middle letter will slide closer to the narrow letter.'

instances.look: Section 05 'Code', HTML only: a strip of 18 code-critical characters (0 1 @ $ ? " % & * - ( [ { ~ ; # ` <), a canvas, and one note per character
instances.ux: Selecting a character shows it in the canvas with its rationale, e.g. the slashed zero or the simplified @; notes point to alternates in section 07
instances.learn: Curate the critique to the glyphs your audience types most, and let notes link straight to the alternate in the configurator

reconstruction.layout: Horizontal radio strip of 18 characters, a large canvas below, a note beside it
reconstruction.typography: Strip ~24px; canvas shows the glyph large (drawn with opentype.js, likely as an outline); notes 12px
reconstruction.behaviour: form#code_form onchange=updateCode; input.code_character radios zero, one, at, …; the canvas redraws per selection
reconstruction.content: '0 (zero): The slashed 0 is easy to tell apart from O at small sizes. Change to a dotted zero in 07 Customize.'
reconstruction.html: form#code_form > fieldset > div > input.code_character[name=code] + label; section#section_5 canvas

instances.look: Section 06 'Distinct', HTML only: the game 'Guess the Character' with Easy, Medium, Hard and Expert radios, pairs of answers such as 'uppercase o' / 'zero' under a confusable glyph, a 'Score: 0/5' and 'Play again?'
instances.feel: A quick quiz that flatters the font
instances.ux: Pick a difficulty, then choose which of two labels matches the shown glyph; the score builds; presumably harder levels shrink the glyphs
instances.learn: Turn a legibility claim into a game: if visitors can tell 0 from O at speed, they have proved the claim themselves

reconstruction.layout: Difficulty radio row, question area with one character and two answer buttons in a list, score line
reconstruction.typography: 12px labels; glyph sample size set by difficulty
reconstruction.behaviour: button.question_button[data-question-index] answers; ten questions per the copy, with the capture state showing 0/5
reconstruction.content: Confusable pairs: O/0, Z/2, b/6, B/8, 5/S

instances.look: Under the game, HTML only: one string of confusable characters, 'tl1I|!ijO0QDØ38B:;.,`‘'"2Z5S7T6b', repeated from 40px down to 8px, each row labelled in rem and px
instances.learn: Use only confusable glyphs for a waterfall: for a coding font, the only size question is when the characters stop being distinct

reconstruction.layout: 8 stacked rows, label then string, left aligned

instances.look: Section 07 'Customize', HTML only: tabs for 8 rival fonts ('Compare different fonts': Commit Mono, Fira Code, JetBrains Mono, Source Code Pro, Cascadia Code, Consolas, Menlo/Meslo, Google Sans Code) and 12 language samples above a code example, with radio ladders for weight, spacing and line height

instances.learn: Keep rivals one keypress from your own font in the same code sample: confidence is persuasive, and the comparison happens where the choice is made

instances.look: Section 07 continued, HTML only: 16 two-state radio rows labelled with their tag and effect (ss01 Ligatures, ss02 Arrows, ss03 Smart case, ss04 Symbol spacing, ss05 Smart kerning; cv01–cv11 alternates, each DEF/ALT), a font-name field, and 'Download custom for dev' and 'Download custom for design'

instances.learn: Bake chosen features into static files in the browser with opentype.js: users of weak tools get the alternates, and no server is needed
